findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is visible to anyone with EC2:DescribeInstanceAttribute permissions or access to the instance metadata service, leading to credential leakage.
The security group allows inbound SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the management plane of the instance to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
Inbound HTTP (port 80) is open to 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls (e.g., WAF, TLS termination), exposing the web service to the entire internet over an unencrypted protocol.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, so data stored on the volume is unencrypted at rest, violating data-at-rest protection requirements.
The EBS snapshot inherits the unencrypted state of its source volume and has no explicit encryption configuration, so the snapshot data (and any copies/shares of it) remains unencrypted at rest.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to instances launched in this subnet, increasing the attack surface by making them directly reachable from the internet.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to instances launched in this subnet, increasing the attack surface by making them directly reachable from the internet.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

findings.issue_category: missing access restriction / public access block
findings.description: The bucket has no bucket policy, ACL restriction, or public access block configuration defined, and force_destroy is enabled, leaving it potentially open to misconfiguration-driven public exposure of flow log data.
